2009-1.sentence: ADHD in a child is rarely a solo act: anxiety and learning trouble often join the room as the child, parent, and teacher keep trading “can’t sit still” for “won’t try,” so stomachaches and decoding failure stay unseen. Treat the relational loop—who is scared, who is ashamed of reading—or the stimulant win will leave the pair still organizing around avoidance.

2009-3.sentence: In borderline relatedness the same person cannot stay both needed and dangerous, so after a fight the coworker is no longer a mixed figure but an all-bad persecutor and a brief psychotic story fills the gap. Sleep and cooling the abandonment storm let the good and bad pieces sit in one relationship again, which is why the plot talk can vanish without a primary psychotic illness.

2009-5.sentence: Thomas and Chess’s difficult child already brings intense mood and irregular sleep and meals into the visit, and the parents and clinician start repeating that same high-volume, poorly timed rhythm—talking over each other, rushing transitions, leaving the room dysregulated. The work is to notice that two-person replay and slow the tempo rather than treat the loudness as badness or low IQ.

2009-6.sentence: Insomnia isn't just a symptom to log — it's often the sign that the part of the mind holding steady through the day, keeping suicidal thoughts passive and distant, has run out of reserve by 3 a.m. That's why pervasive insomnia predicts emergent suicidality better than being male or over 65: ask about sleep the way you'd ask about a gun in the house.

2009-10.sentence: A fiduciary relationship runs on trust, not on a fee, a favor, or a signed note — the patient has to rely on you because you know more and hold more power than they do. Every time a kickback or a side incentive tempts a treatment decision, that trust is the actual thing being spent.

2009-11.sentence: Mother’s hospitalization and missed medicine drop this patient with schizophrenia onto Erikson’s earliest task—can daily functioning be trusted to hold—not onto insight or identity work. Supportive therapy’s goal is to restabilize that functioning and strengthen existing defenses, not to raise self-awareness, agree for self-esteem, or only fix the environment.

2009-12.sentence: Higher-level histrionic organization has a working conscience: seductiveness is subtly appealing rather than raw impulse, overestimated intimacy, or uncontained transference heat. That same guilt-and-limit capacity lets the patient reflect, keep reality testing, and feel mixed about the flirtation when you set a frame.

2009-17.sentence: The wish to feel something in ten superficial wrist cuts collides with a death wish she half-owns (“easier if I were dead”), and recent alcohol abuse is the drive that melts the last prohibition so the cut can go deeper than she meant. Sexual-abuse history, borderline traits, or having never cut ten times before do not outrank that chemical disinhibition when you decide who needs the locked door tonight.

2009-19.sentence: The fluent lecture about cars and computers can fool you into reading this as a bright, if odd, kid — but what's actually missing isn't knowledge, it's the back-and-forth: reading the other child's face, pausing, taking a turn. That's why it isn't shyness in hiding; it's a mind that can talk at another person all day without ever quite joining them.

2009-20.sentence: Lithium carbonate is not only an ion; it is the reliable adult who stays after a suicide attempt and becomes a chemical secure base the patient can protest toward instead of dying. Prescribe it as proximity you can count on—blood levels, clinic visits, the same bottle—so the person does not have to use death to regulate when the mood drops.

2009-22.sentence: When OCD arrives in bursts with bipolar mood, do not excavate every contamination thought as if the ego can use uncovering; support first, stabilize sleep and mood, then decide how much ritual talk this mind can metabolize. Technique follows prognosis: episodic, mood-tied rituals need containing structure more than interpretation until the bipolar swing is quieter.

2009-25.sentence: When parents bring the invisible friend into the consult as a problem, they are already asking you to join a two-person drama about who is allowed to play. Name the friend as ordinary preschool make-believe so the family does not have to enact a medical crisis around a healthy 4-year-old’s companion.

2009-26.sentence: The needle on the tray can split the recovering heroin user: one part sits for labs, another is already back in the vein. Treat the craving as a classically conditioned flash, not as proof they secretly decided to use, so the split can be talked about instead of acted.

2009-27.sentence: Amphetamine can blow out the ego’s hold on reality testing, so flashing computer messages feel like real threats and a knife feels like self-care. Until that state settles, you contain agitation and weapon talk; you do not interpret the messages as if the observing ego were still online.

2009-28.sentence: Pramipexole-driven gambling and hypersexuality do not wait for a planned ending; the dopamine agonist has already removed the brake. The work is a firm limit—name the drug, stop or change it, and do not treat the new appetites as a character flaw you can interpret away while the agonist is still on.

2009-29.sentence: Delirium tremens at 36 hours after the bleed is not a moment for a trial comment about drinking or insight. Psychological mindedness returns only after benzos, vitals, and seizure care restore a mind that can hear a remark.

2009-35.sentence: Late arrivals and one-word CBT answers are data on alliance, the factor most tied to outcome—not on whether you recited the manual. A trial comment—“does this work even feel like yours?”—tests if they can see their part in the stall instead of only taking more homework.

2009-36.sentence: Eight hospitalizations and never three weeks in placement means the usual model — show up to your appointment, stay engaged — has already failed this man. Assertive community treatment works because the team goes to the street instead of waiting for him to arrive and stay; clozapine, CBT, or ECT can't fix a system that still expects that.

2009-37.sentence: Alogia here is speech that names almost nothing—white, things, I am—so the interviewer’s job is to hold the dread of an empty mind without stuffing it with extra questions. You contain (take in the raw feeling and give it back in a thinkable form) the poverty of thought by reflecting how little can be said, rather than chasing a hidden sentence that was never formed.

2009-38.sentence: Premature ejaculation so often hits as a competence injury: the man feels he cannot last long enough to be a good lover, so shame, not desire, starts running the bedroom. A self-psychological stance mirrors that he is still a sexual person whose timing failed him, instead of confirming the collapse of self-esteem that makes him avoid partners.

2009-39.sentence: Personality change with early falls and dysphagia is progressive supranuclear palsy dismantling motor and frontal circuits — it is not the patient 'giving up' or a character change the family could have prevented. Naming the neurologic loss keeps a grieving family's guilt ('we should have pushed him harder') from being mistaken for the actual diagnosis.

2009-41.sentence: Charles Bonnet hallucinations aren't a sign of losing your mind — they're the visual system filling the blank left by macular degeneration with vivid, unbidden pictures, while insight stays fully intact. Naming that plainly is often the most therapeutic thing you can do: it turns a private fear of 'going crazy' into a known, explainable consequence of vision loss.

2009-44.sentence: The frame is diagnostic honesty: you do not treat cartoon-soldier visions as a psychosis ticket that would lock the patient into antipsychotics and a schizophrenia narrative. Conversion hallucinations stay childish and fantastic so the symptom can speak without becoming a second diagnosis you then have to “manage” with drugs and a locked unit.

2009-47.sentence: A five-year-old who says Mom is watching from the sky after the crash is using the only insight his age allows—not a trial interpretation of denial you would offer an adult. Psychological mindedness here is the child’s concrete afterlife story; you listen for play and sleep, you do not confront him as if he should already see death the way you do.

2009-48.sentence: The double bind is class and loyalty as a third in the room: go to college (become someone else) and do not spend the family’s money (stay our child). Betty cannot obey both messages without betraying either mobility or the household that cannot afford her leaving.

2009-55.sentence: The neighbor-poisoning conviction sits on a collapse of basic trust (Erikson’s first task): the world next door is no longer safe enough to leave, so the day is spent at the window and the night is spent awake. Empathy without arguing the delusion is how you become a usable other—someone who can be leaned on while trust in the neighbor, and in one’s own perception, is still wrecked.

2009-56.sentence: Hippocrates’ four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) moved “mental disease” out of a purely moral ledger—sin, vice, a harsh conscience that must be punished—and into a bodily imbalance that a physician could treat. Black bile as the ancestor of melancholia is the historical reminder that we still risk treating depression as a character defect rather than a state that needs care.

2009-57.sentence: Megadosing vitamin B6 to 'fend off Alzheimer's' is often less about the vitamin and more about a patient trying to seize control of a fear they can't otherwise manage — aging and cognitive decline. The burning, tingling neuropathy that results is a hard lesson that this kind of self-treatment can't substitute for actually facing that fear with a clinician.

2009-58.sentence: Jung’s introversion/extroversion names how a person holds good and bad: energy turned toward inner objects and inner scenes, or toward people and events outside. Calling a quiet patient “introverted” in Jung’s sense is only fair if you mean that inward object-world, not that they have split off the outer other as dangerous or worthless.

2009-59.sentence: In bulimia nervosa the mind that asks “will therapy work?” can usually use a structured, here-and-now method more than deep uncovering: CBT targets regular eating, binge–purge cycles, and rigid food and shape rules. Save exploratory or psychoanalytic work for later, if at all; first give a technique with evidence this ego can actually use.

2009-60.sentence: A forensic fee that is a percentage of the plaintiff’s award ties the psychiatrist’s worth and “ideal expert” shine to the size of the win, so the evaluator needs the examinee to be damaged. Flat, hourly, or retainer pay keeps self-esteem in competence and honesty, not in mirroring a victory.

2009-61.sentence: The mid-session drift is not just boredom; it is the hour pouring a raw, unnameable feeling into you so it does not have to stay inside the patient (Bion’s evacuation). Your first job is to sit with that sleepy, wandering state long enough to name it in yourself—containment—before you speak, apologize, or cut the session short.

2009-65.sentence: ECT can be dramatically effective for severe psychotic depression, but patients often experience the trade differently than clinicians do — it's a treatment that also takes something, memory. Cognitive impairment is the side effect most likely to make someone hesitate or stop, so it deserves as much of the informed-consent conversation as the benefit does.

2009-69.sentence: One week after his wife dies he still works and shows up socially, so the ego can still hold grief, sleep, and appetite without a full collapse. On this older rule, two months of the same anhedonia is the point where that remaining strength is no longer enough and major depression is diagnosed.

2009-71.sentence: The teen who sleeps eighteen hours, eats when awake, and looks dull recruits you to become the parent who keeps shaking him—or the doctor who feels bored and writes him off. That countertransference dullness belongs to Kleine–Levin (normal NREM/REM, long sleep, hyperphagia), not to narcolepsy or apnea; do not enact the withdrawal by stopping the workup.

2009-77.sentence: Hours of lock-checking are the wish to be perfectly safe colliding with a harsh inner ban on any leftover risk; the ritual is the compromise, not the cure. First-line CBT (exposure and response prevention) puts that collision on the table so the prohibition can be practiced against, rather than endlessly obeyed.

2009-80.sentence: IPT's 'sick role' gives a patient explicit permission to be unwell — a formal counterweight to the guilt of thinking rest or asking for help is just selfishness. Naming the diagnosis isn't a label for its own sake; it's what lets someone step back from an interpersonal role they've been unable to put down on their own.

2009-83.sentence: An insurer pushing to discharge a patient you still consider unsafe is pressure on the relationship, not just on the bed — cave to it and the patient learns that being sent away is what happens when things get hard. Keep the person in the hospital as long as medical safety requires; the insurer's timeline is not the treatment plan.

2009-84.sentence: Whether PTSD follows the fire tracks how close and how severe the exposure was—the trapped, injured survivor faces a bigger developmental overload than the relative who only heard the story. Childhood history and support matter less here than whether the ego’s current capacity was simply outgunned by proximity and dose of trauma.

2009-85.sentence: A standing risperidone order can function as a moral shortcut: the team’s conscience is soothed by “doing something” about frightening hallucinations while the patient’s Lewy-body rigidity and falls absorb the cost. Hold the guilt in the room—name that protecting gait and cognition is the ethical act, not quieting voices with a D2 blocker that this brain cannot tolerate.

2009-86.sentence: Adolescence is Erikson’s identity-versus-role-confusion work; a loaded gun in the house turns a still-forming self into a one-decision tragedy. The most identity-preserving prevention is not a lecture or a hotline but removing firearms so the identity crisis cannot end in a completed act.

2009-88.sentence: Four months after the spouse’s cancer death, self-blame and “I should have died instead” sit in Klein’s depressive position: he is trying to repair a loved object he feels he destroyed, not merely “normal grief.” Antidepressant plus psychotherapy holds that guilt so it can become mourning rather than a demand that he be punished in her place.

2009-89.sentence: Peek-a-boo works because the infant is developing object permanence — the understanding that the hidden face still exists and will come back, which is what makes the reunion feel like a small, repeatable proof that people don't disappear. It's testing that one cognitive milestone, nothing broader about who is playing the game.

2009-91.sentence: Invite the quiet members to say what they actually felt when the room went still, so the patient can use the group as a secure base instead of treating silence as proof of abandonment. Consensual validation is proximity-seeking done in words: comparing the rejection story with other people’s inner states until the distortion loosens.

2009-97.sentence: This sits on Erikson’s generativity-versus-stagnation work of midlife: she is re-choosing what faith she will pass on, not dissolving who she is. The guilt that she is “acting against her moral beliefs” is the cost of that adult identity revision, which is why DSM codes a religious or spiritual problem rather than an identity disorder.

2009-98.sentence: Mother’s “our disease” and answering for the boy is a fused conscience: his colitis pain and her worry are treated as one moral unit, so he never gets a private “I.” Minuchin calls that enmeshment—boundaries so thin that guilt and caretaking replace a separate self.

2009-99.sentence: Cultural identity isn't fixed at birth or handed down by race — it shifts with acculturation, how much of a new culture's language, values, and ways of understanding illness a person has taken in over time. Ask about that directly instead of assuming that belonging to a group tells you someone's ethnic identity.

2009-100.sentence: A patient who suddenly distrusts the therapy itself — 'my coworkers are listening to the tapes' — is telling you the office no longer feels like a safe, sealed space. Asking for the details behind that fear keeps you inside the relationship and gathering real data, instead of reassuring him out of it or reaching for a diagnosis first.

2009-102.sentence: Twelve-step facilitation enacts the addiction as a disease you stop fighting alone: acceptance and surrender to help beyond oneself become the couplet in the room. That is a two-person repetition of “I cannot control this,” unlike CBT, MET, or dynamic therapy, which keep more of the fight inside the patient’s will.

2009-105.sentence: A history of postpartum psychosis isn't just a risk statistic to flag — for many women it was a genuine collapse of their sense of themselves as capable, at the exact moment they needed to feel most competent. Hoping 'this time will be different' isn't a plan; real confidence going into the next delivery comes from planning around that history, not wishing it away.

2009-106.sentence: A trial comment—“the oral meperidine is simply weaker milligram for milligram than the IM shots”—tests whether she can see her part in the panic as pharmacology, not as craving. If she can use that, psychological mindedness is intact; if she can only hear accusation, insight has not arrived yet.

2009-107.sentence: Hypokalemia, hypochloremic alkalosis, and an amylase spike with normal lipase are the body keeping score of how much purging has already cost it. Medical stabilization of the binge-purge cycle has to come first here; the body won't wait for the patient to feel ready for insight.

2009-108.sentence: The cholinesterase inhibitor will not give childhood memories back; wanting it to is the transference wish that you become the parent who restores what was lost. Your countertransference urge to “fix” visuospatial skill or reverse the dementia is that same recruitment—stay with reducing agitation, not with being the miracle.

2009-111.sentence: Condensation is how a dream can let you have three feelings at once without feeling any of them fully: your teacher, your parent, and your supervisor can all show up as a single dream figure, compressing the wish or fear attached to each into one manageable image. That's the dream doing economy of representation, not necessarily hiding anything.

2009-113.sentence: Naming primary autism as the infant’s first state is adult denial of what the newborn already does: attend to faces, voices, and cross-modal cues that start attachment. The consultation that watches gaze and vocal turn-taking undoes that denial by treating the infant as already a partner, not a sealed-off mind.

2009-114.sentence: The best malpractice shield is not the no-harm contract or the withheld risky drug; it is the two-person pattern of talking through benefits, harms, and how to reach the team. Suit risk drops when both people have already practiced staying in the relationship after a bad outcome is named.

2009-115.sentence: A reading-disabled 11-year-old who also has inattentive ADHD cannot use uncovering; the ego is already overloaded by lost materials, missed multistep directions, and unfinished work. Technique stays supportive: scaffold attention and reading load first, then add insight only if school function actually holds.

2009-119.sentence: MS depression is not a badge of lesion load or interferon virtue; it is a collapse of self-esteem and felt competence that still answers to antidepressants. Mirror the low mood as real depression, treat it, and the patient’s idealizable rehab self can come back online instead of being swallowed by fatigue.

2009-121.sentence: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (the adducting eye stalls, the abducting eye nystagmus) is a concrete hit to reality testing: the world literally doubles and tilts, so the first ego job is naming the finding as a medial-longitudinal-fasciculus lesion, not as “I’m going crazy.” Affect tolerance then means sitting with a probable multiple-sclerosis diagnosis without either denying the diplopia or flooding into catastrophe before the MRI and the rest of the exam are in.

2009-124.sentence: Empathy is taking in what the patient actually feels — 'everyone thinks I'm lazy, but I'm exhausted' — and reflecting it back as their experience, not swapping it for what you imagine you'd feel in their shoes (that's identification) or feeling sorry for them (that's sympathy). The skill is staying inside their perspective while still being yourself.

2009-126.sentence: A 36-year-old with migraine and a posterior-cerebral-artery infarct after oral contraceptives cannot use deep uncovering of “why me” until the vascular fact is held: estrogen plus migraine is the likely mechanism. Technique is supportive first—stop the pill, name the stroke risk in plain language—and only later, if ego can bear it, work the meaning of losing vision or independence.

2009-128.sentence: Intellectual disability does not invent a private catalog of mental illness; the same mood, anxiety, psychosis, and behavioral syndromes still arrive, only later or harder to hear. What often never quite arrives is a reliable way to name those syndromes instead of folding them into the cognitive deficit.

2009-129.sentence: Daytime alcohol is doing night-shift work the circadian clock will not: forcing sleep after a duty cycle that wrecked alertness. Relieving the night shift first withdraws the symptom’s job before you load on disulfiram, naltrexone, or an antidepressant.

2009-130.sentence: Forced medication is a technique choice that suspends autonomy—the patient’s right to refuse this antipsychotic after a capacity talk. Uncovering “why they refuse” comes after you know whether this ego can still hold a specific informed no.

2009-132.sentence: Psychoeducation is containment: the family is handed facts, meds, sleep, and problem-solving so they stop receiving the patient’s projected chaos as if it were their own failure. Calm guidelines invite depressive concern—repair and support—rather than a paranoid hunt for who caused the schizophrenia.

2009-133.sentence: Flattened pitch and wrong stress are a speech-motor loss, not a mood or affect problem, so do not treat the person as emotionally empty because the music of speech is gone. If you hear “cold” or “dead,” check whether you are reacting to dysprosody rather than to what they actually think and feel.

2009-135.sentence: Late-life depression more often uses a psychotic story—poisoned food, ruined family—to give shape to collapse, instead of the early-onset confession of worthlessness. Ask what the delusion is doing: it may be holding terror that the person cannot yet say as ordinary sad mood.

2009-136.sentence: Feeling like his 'spirit left his body' three weeks after watching someone die is a dissociative symptom, not a sign this man is fracturing into a new identity — it's how an overwhelmed mind protects itself in the acute aftermath of horror. The diagnostic task now is mostly about time: the same numbness and intrusive dreams get relabeled PTSD only if they're still there past the one-month mark.

2009-138.sentence: She can want and climax alone, so you are not meeting low desire; you are meeting a no to the husband as initiator. Notice if you become the gynecologist who found “nothing wrong,” or the husband who keeps approaching—both recruitments miss the aversion itself.

2009-139.sentence: Marginalization — no real footing in the culture of origin and none built in the new one — leaves a person without a story of where they belong, and that gap doesn't stay abstract; it shows up as elevated risk for suicide, alcohol, and other substance use. For an adolescent caught between two worlds, that felt homelessness is the risk factor, not any single event.

2009-141.sentence: In childhood-onset schizophrenia the ego functions that should arrive in latency—stable reality testing, play that stays play, a school self that can recover after a bad week—never quite lock in, so the course is typically chronic and unremitting rather than episodic. The developmental point is not a later “break” after a formed personality, but a psychotic process that occupies the years when those capacities were supposed to consolidate.

2009-145.sentence: Without object constancy—the inner sense that the same person stays whole when the schedule shifts—the clinician who changes an appointment is no longer a mixed, reliable other and becomes a dismissive controller. The wish to cling and the wish to attack then have nowhere to live except in the accusation that the office is persecuting them.

2009-151.sentence: An aging liver that clears antipsychotics more slowly is also a weaker ego for affect and impulse: the same milligrams that a younger patient can metabolize become a flood the older patient cannot hold. Start low so the person can still test reality and ride out agitation without the drug itself becoming the next insult to coping.

2009-152.sentence: Wanting to stay on valproate through a first-trimester window is often denial dressed as stability: the neural-tube risk is set aside so the familiar mood stabilizer does not have to be mourned. Name the defense and the folate/teratogen fact together so planning a switch is grief work, not a sudden rupture.

2009-157.sentence: By 12 months, a baby can check a parent's face before deciding whether an unfamiliar toy, person, or drop-off is safe to approach — using someone else's emotional reaction to navigate an ambiguous situation, before they can name their own fear in words. That look toward the caregiver is social referencing, one of the earliest signs a baby is reading other minds, not just faces.

2009-158.sentence: Kagan’s inhibited infant is stuck on Erikson’s autonomy-versus-shame task: novelty feels like a test they will fail, so they freeze rather than try. That same shame-anxiety line is why early behavioral inhibition tracks later anxiety disorders, not ADHD, learning, mood, or conduct.

2009-161.sentence: On the TAT the patient dumps inner figures into the picture—who is attacking, who must be repaired—so you hear paranoid-schizoid threat versus depressive concern without them owning it as theirs. That is projective identification onto the scene: the story carries the split so they do not have to feel it as their own.

2009-163.sentence: Name the mismatch between “I’m fine about my sibling’s drinking” and the crack of anger in the voice; that is confrontation, not interpretation of hidden meaning. Use it only if this mind can hear the affect without collapsing—otherwise stay with support and let the feeling stay unnamed until the ego can hold it.

2009-164.sentence: Avoidant and schizoid both sit far from people; the relational difference is that the avoidant still wants closeness and is organizing around feared rejection, not around no appetite for others. Treat the pattern as two-person: invitations declined are about expected humiliation, so the work is safety of contact, not “teaching” social skills to someone who never desired them.

2009-166.sentence: Direct conditioning after this man’s own crash means the ego now treats driving as danger he cannot yet titrate; panic and job-threatening avoidance show affect and impulse regulation are overloaded. Technique is graded exposure that rebuilds reality testing (“the car is not the collision”), not insight about why he “chose” to stop driving.

2009-167.sentence: Hopping to irrelevant topics right when a painful subject comes up is resistance — the patient stays in the chair but leaves the feeling behind. Name the move gently rather than as an accusation: 'we were talking about the death, and then the conversation moved to work' invites the patient back without shaming them for having left.

2009-168.sentence: Hyperactivity fading by adolescence while inattention and disorganization stay means the room may still fill with late work, lost papers, and interruptions even as the body sits still. That leftover mess can become an enactment: you chase, they scramble, and the old ADHD pair repeats unless you treat the remaining symptoms as the task, not as willful chaos.

2009-179.sentence: Wraparound keeps the child near the people who already function as a secure base so aggression does not get solved by sending them away to a hospital or residence. The goal is proximity and a usable home team, not a new placement that treats separation as treatment.

2009-180.sentence: The wish is to be steered through every task while the doctor is gone; the prohibition is against a loud, entitled protest, so the distress stays panicky, withdrawn, and politely timed to the vacation. That collision—need for a caretaker versus not daring to rage—is dependent, not the storm of a borderline abandonment scene.

2009-181.sentence: When carbamazepine speeds up methadone's clearance, the withdrawal that follows can look to a skeptical team exactly like relapse or drug-seeking, when it's really a drug interaction. Don't let pharmacokinetics get mistaken for a moral failure in a patient who's already fighting stigma.

2009-182.sentence: In a school-age child, irritability is often nameless dread that has not yet become thinkable sadness; the household and classroom get the raw evacuation of a depressive affect that cannot be named. Containment here means asking about anhedonia, sleep, appetite, and energy so the argumentativeness can be metabolized into a mood diagnosis rather than left as opposition.

2009-185.sentence: In an otherwise typically developing preschooler, hitting often does the work the sentence cannot: it discharges a conflict the child cannot yet put into words. Limited verbal ability is the meaning of the aggression—build language and pause at the trigger so the fist is not left as the only available speech.

2009-187.sentence: The conscience can demand a pill for a problem that is already resolving, as if doing nothing were negligence. Transient global amnesia wants observation, not memantine, olanzapine, or lorazepam, because the moral task here is to tolerate a scary blank without medicating it away.

2009-188.sentence: The payday-craving link can feel like proof the old pattern is permanent, but each payday he gets through without using is the cue losing its grip — extinction, not exception. Don't let a spike in craving talk either of you into believing relapse is inevitable.

2009-189.sentence: Denial here is not a speech about drinking; it is the empty fridge while Korsakoff memory loss keeps the body from registering that it is starving. A nutritious diet is the confrontation that actually matters, because thiamine and calories, not an NSAID or a cholinesterase inhibitor, are what slow the slide toward alcohol-related dementia.

2009-191.sentence: Retentive encopresis is a plumbing problem before it's a meaning problem — no amount of talking through the 'why' will move an impacted colon. Psychoeducation and laxatives come first; the shame and control issues can wait until the body is working again.

2009-194.sentence: In individual DBT the psychiatrist is the relationship that both feeds and withholds: warmth is given, but the “pill” of care is never a substitute for the patient doing the next skill. Nurture without a demand to self-help becomes poison; a demand without nurture becomes a dead prescription.

2009-196.sentence: This patient can describe feeling frustrated but may resist hearing that some of the blankness is his brain's wiring — periventricular white matter disease — not just his mood. Naming both together, gently, tests whether he can hold a cause besides 'I'm just depressed.'

2009-198.sentence: Hypochondriasis takes the raw dread of dying and bodily failure — feelings too frightening to simply feel — and converts them into a fixation on disease that can be hunted down and checked. A clean workup should calm that fear, but often it can't, because the fear was never really about the test result.

2009-201.sentence: Motivational interviewing first mirrors the OCD patient’s competence—naming what washing still “works” for—before anyone asks them to stop. Idealizing the therapist as the one who “gets it” rebuilds self-esteem enough that exposure can later be chosen rather than assigned.

2009-202.sentence: Clang associations recruit you into a rhyming partner: “bright / light / flight / right” asks you to chase sound instead of meaning, safety, or sleep. Notice the countertransference pull to finish the couplet or smile at the cleverness; that is the transferential bid to become an audience, not an examiner.

2009-203.sentence: The “special / needs really good treatment” handoff is an unremembered split already repeating in the referral itself. Anticipate splitting—holding both doctors as all-good or all-bad—rather than probing old boundary crossings or promising extra gentleness that enacts the same unrepresented demand.

2009-204.sentence: Termination of parental rights is driven far more often by neglect than by abuse — by a parent who never became the reliable presence keeping the child fed, safe, and taken to the doctor, not by a single dramatic act. When evaluating these families, look for that missing steady provision, not just for injuries.

2009-205.sentence: Histrionic affect is loud, but the superego—the inner prosecutor that says “I am late, I am failing, I am unlovable”—is often what just exploded. Ask him what happened before the rage so conscience can be examined instead of discharged as a divorce edict.

2009-207.sentence: Emergency medicine's high substance-use rate isn't just about access — for a job that demands you stay sharp and unshaken through shift after shift of crisis, the substance often functions as a private, unsanctioned way of holding yourself together when there's no one to hand that job to.

2009-208.sentence: The two-year-old parked next to the other toddler's truck isn't ignoring her — parallel play is its own real developmental stage, sharing the space without yet sharing the game. Push for 'let's play together' too early and you're asking for a skill the two-year-old mind hasn't built yet.

2009-209.sentence: A 60-year-old with flattening apathy and a low B12 can look like she's psychologically checked out, withdrawn from her own life — but this is a metabolic brain running low on fuel, not a defense. Check the B12 before you go looking for what she might be avoiding.

2009-212.sentence: The wish is still for a quick dopaminergic lift; the prohibition is not to hand a divertible stimulant to an adolescent who already sold someone else’s pills. Atomoxetine treats ADHD without feeding that collision, so the drive can be named in therapy instead of being swallowed or sold.

2009-214.sentence: The condemning voice is raw, undigested badness dumped into the child’s mind rather than held until it can be thought as depression. Containment means you name major depressive disorder and stay with the irritability and guilt instead of evacuating the problem into oppositionality or childhood-onset schizophrenia.

2009-216.sentence: Circumstantiality still gets to the point; it just cannot close without first unloading weather, traffic, and breakfast. A trial comment—“you took the long way, and then you said sleep”—tests whether they can see that extra loop as theirs, not as the world’s necessary inventory.

2009-217.sentence: Reporting a driver with progressing dementia is a termination of a freedom, and you cannot rush past the state’s legal clock by inventing half-limits like daylight-only or no-highways. Check the statute first; talking with the patient is the work, but unilateral “just be careful” is a wish that the lost capacity will wait.

2009-219.sentence: Blunted affect is something two people feel together: the face goes still and you start working harder to keep the room alive. Hallucinations, thought insertion, and control delusions are additions; this negative symptom is a missing interpersonal signal, not a story the patient is telling you.

2009-221.sentence: The anesthesiologist’s falling asleep in the OR, weight gain, and unrefreshing nights look like a conscience problem—overwork, burnout, a sanctioned gap in self-care—but the harsher verdict is medical: breathing-related sleep disorder. Guilt about “not refueling” can hide apnea; a negative urine screen does not absolve the airway.

2009-223.sentence: When the fight lives only in the dolls, it is often an unrepresented state: something that cannot yet be remembered in words is being repeated in play. Name the dolls’ anger without pinning it on the child so the scene can become thinkable instead of a forced confession.

2009-224.sentence: Trial competence is a frame problem, not a diagnosis: the court cannot proceed if the person cannot even understand the charges. Psychosis, old hospitalizations, or M’Naughten-style questions about wrongfulness do not by themselves collapse that frame.

2009-225.sentence: Copropraxia looks like a rude message, but it is a tic: an intrusive obscene gesture that is not answering the room. Do not treat it as a parapraxis or a wish; Tourette’s motor burst arrives before meaning does.

2009-226.sentence: The M’Naughten rule asks whether illness wrecked knowledge of the nature of the act or that it was wrong—whether the moral faculty could still judge. Durham, irresistible impulse, and the Model Penal Code test other parts of the mind; this one is knowing, not stopping the impulse.

2009-227.sentence: Little Albert’s fear is a manufactured pairing of a stimulus with a loud noise, not a symbol the infant needed. Nonmaleficence forbids installing that phobia so classical conditioning can look true.

2009-229.sentence: An IQ of 65 with a sixth-grade ceiling isn't just a number inside this teenager — it plays out in the daily fit between him and the adults around him. When parents and teachers keep expecting typical-seventeen-year-old pace, he fails, they push harder, and nobody stops to match the demand to what he can actually do.

2009-230.sentence: Piaget cared less about whether a child gave the right answer than about how they got there — the reasoning process is the developmental story. When assessing a child's thinking, watch the method they use to solve the problem, not just whether they land on the correct one.

2009-231.sentence: The lucrative investment offer is a test of the frame, and the live third in the room is status: older successful businessman, younger male psychiatrist, money as the language of who is on top. Decline the deal and stay curious about the seduction—he is asking whether you can be bought, rivaled, or turned into a junior partner instead of a therapist.

2009-235.sentence: The isolated voice is often a two-person move: the preschooler puts the fear into a sound so a caregiver can hear it and help settle it. Anxiety is the shared climate that makes that scene, not a one-mind break into schizophrenia.

2009-239.sentence: The husband’s “everything is fine” is already the enactment: the two of you are living the denial instead of naming the infant-risk. Involuntary admission interrupts that cover story when she feels an “evil force” and cannot keep the baby safe.

2009-241.sentence: Sullivan's interpersonal psychiatry treats anxiety as a signal that relatedness is threatened, so ego strength is the capacity to stay in contact without collapsing into panic or rage. Security operations—his word for the automatic ways we manage that anxiety—are the patient's coping, not a character defect to shame.

2009-242.sentence: The limp arm is conversion as a defense: the mind knocks the limb offline so the rage impulse never reaches a punch. That is primary gain—the symptom itself reduces inner conflict; it is not a performance for disability papers.

2009-243.sentence: Echolalia turns the interview into an enactment: the patient cannot author speech, so your words bounce back parrot-fashion and you become the only speaker in the room. Name that two-person freeze as catatonic, then look for the rest of the motor picture rather than arguing content with a mute mind.

2009-244.sentence: Substance-related disorder, not schizophrenia or mania, is the most common psychiatric finding in people who assault others—so technique starts with intoxication, withdrawal, and access, not uncovering childhood rage. Insight work on a wet brain is theater; support, detox, and risk containment come first.

2009-245.sentence: After the affair he can hold only a bad object: she must hurt exactly as he hurts, and there is no mixed picture of a loved wife who also betrayed him. That revenge plan is not a delusion you treat on a locked unit; send him back to law enforcement because the threat is specific and the mind is organized around punishment, not psychosis.

2009-247.sentence: A no-self-harm contract is a one-person charm; the legally protective act is the two of you actually thinking the risk together—ideation, intent, plan, means, attempts, intoxication, stressors, and reasons for living. Write that conversation down so the work is not “I extracted a promise” but “we named what could kill them and what still holds them.”

2009-251.sentence: Late-life “depression” that is mostly hypersomnia and unrefreshing sleep in morbid obesity often means the night is failing the self, not that the character is weak. Polysomnography is the honest mirror: it shows whether apnea is stealing competence and mood, so you treat sleep rather than idealize another antidepressant.

2009-252.sentence: After a myocardial infarction, depression—not mania, panic, albumin, or even ejection fraction in this comparison—is the strongest predictor of death, so the trial comment is about their part: withdrawal from rehab, anhedonia, hopelessness. Psychological mindedness here is seeing that the sad, guilty, sleepless self is not a side note to the infarct but a risk factor you can name and treat.

2009-254.sentence: Projective identification is not just “they dumped a feeling on you.” The patient disavows a helpless, unhelpable self and then recruits you—via insistence that no clinician can understand—to live that identity in countertransference. If you start believing you are uniquely incompetent, you are wearing their discarded representation, not discovering a new fact about your skill.

2009-255.sentence: The finding is not more genetic loading or “minority risk”; it is greater vulnerability to the same stressful events once class already depletes reserve. A harsh superego—the inner judge that says poverty is a character defect—lets the system treat exposure as deserved rather than as a load the ego cannot metabolize.

2009-256.sentence: An overvalued idea is a wish for certainty about the defect colliding with a prohibition that still works: when challenged, the person can admit it may not be true. The symptom (hours of mirrors, social avoidance) holds both the drive to be rid of the imagined flaw and the remaining grip of reality testing that a delusion would have already surrendered.

2009-259.sentence: Kohut’s move is empathic validation: you first show that the patient’s experience of being unseen is real, not a tantrum to be confronted. A missed callback can land as a selfobject failure—the therapist briefly stops being the mirroring presence that holds the self together.

2009-260.sentence: IPT leaves the childhood split alone and treats today’s lunch table as the live relationship problem. You help her use the friendships she already has as good objects she can actually lean on, instead of treating every coworker as a rejecting other.

2009-261.sentence: Carbamazepine induces CYP3A4 and can chew through a previously solid 10 mg of haloperidol. The returning voices are the blood level falling, not a new internal collapse of the mind.

2009-263.sentence: An AA sponsor is not the meeting chair or the chip-passer; they are one experienced member who guides the program one-to-one. That pairing sits on Erikson’s generativity: someone further along offers care so the newcomer can rebuild an adult identity without alcohol.

2009-267.sentence: At 3 a.m. you are being recruited to become the person who finally shuts the ward up, and that feeling pushes you toward quetiapine, diphenhydramine, or a benzodiazepine. This item wants zolpidem first for insomnia in a 78-year-old with dementia, so name the countertransference hunger to over-sedate before you reach for an antipsychotic.

2009-268.sentence: In Capgras the face is seen, but the warm recognition that should attach to father never arrives, so the mind solves it by calling him an impostor. What cannot be felt as “this is my father” gets repeated as a stranger standing in his place.

2009-269.sentence: The idea of the father kicking the puppy is allowed; the rage, horror, and grief are not. Isolation of affect is that split: the drive-laden feeling is cut away so the story can be told as if it were weather.

2009-270.sentence: An advance directive is a conversation two people can still have while the patient is competent, not a monologue you start after life support has already changed the pair. Talk when both of you can still think together about future decisions.

2009-271.sentence: Flooding works only if the therapist stays a secure base: someone close enough that the patient can protest, borrow calm, and not flee the 15-minute talk. The unknown staff are the feared crowd; you are the person the patient uses to regulate while they stay in the room.

2009-273.sentence: Alcohol splits the mind: the suicidal line is there, but the person who can name a plan, use judgment, or make a pact is not in the chair yet. Observe and reevaluate when he is sober so you interview the whole mind, not the intoxicated fragment.

2009-275.sentence: Pictures of the nanny let the child keep a good object in mind and feel sad, which is Klein’s depressive concern: missing someone without having to hate or erase them. A quick replacement nanny would be a manic patch—plug the hole instead of letting the child repair the loss.

2009-276.sentence: An elevated MCV often tells a truer story than the interview does — the patient says 'not that much,' while the lab already shows the pattern of heavy drinking. Use the number as an opening to ask again, gently, rather than making him pick one version of the story on the spot.

2009-277.sentence: A three-year-old checking mom's face at the curb isn't being overly cautious — social referencing is exactly how young children are supposed to borrow an adult's read on danger before their own judgment is ready. That's a normal developmental tool, not a deficit to train out of them early.

2009-281.sentence: The antidepressant becomes a third object in the room—rescuer, poison, proof of weakness—not a neutral chemical. Optimal work holds the good and bad of the pill inside the same treatment relationship so the patient does not split “real therapy” from “just meds.”

2009-284.sentence: Competence is the part of the mind that can stay in the chair while you list risks, benefits, and alternatives; dissociation is the vertical split where that part clocks out even though the body signs. If she cannot hold the information long enough to choose freely, you do not have informed consent—you have a signature from the absent half.

2009-287.sentence: Slot machines run on variable-ratio reinforcement — you never know which pull will pay off — and that unpredictability is exactly what makes the behavior so hard to extinguish, harder than if every pull paid the same. It's the same principle behind why intermittent hope keeps someone chasing a losing hand long after a sure thing would have made them stop.

2009-288.sentence: Double depression changes the frame: years of dysthymia plus a new major episode with hopelessness and suicide talk is not a Tuesday-afternoon “mild dysphoria” visit. You hold time, safety, and the limit on leaving him in bed with a chronic-only diagnosis while the acute risk is in the room.

2009-289.sentence: Telling a patient in pain that a triptan is off the table because of his heart isn't a refusal to help — it's naming a real limit before the drug does the vasoconstricting for you. Say the reason out loud so declining feels like protecting him, not withholding relief.

2009-290.sentence: During a blackout the person genuinely isn't laying down memory, even while acting normal and awake — so when he says 'I don't remember,' that's not evasion, it's a true gap. The missing hours have to come from someone who was actually there, not from pushing him to 'try harder' to recall.

2009-292.sentence: Billing for a missed visit is only ethical when the fee was already spelled out in the agreement you both signed — not a judgment call made after the fact about whether the excuse was good enough. Keeping it in a pre-set written policy turns it into a business term instead of a punishment.

2009-293.sentence: Lateral medullary stroke in a 56-year-old who smokes with diabetes and hypertension is a vascular event, not “anxious dizziness.” Class and smoking history sit in the room as a third: do not let the consult become a story about panic in people who “don’t take care of themselves.” Hoarseness, ipsilateral face pin loss, and veering left keep the body, not the stereotype, in charge.

2009-296.sentence: The adolescent is recruiting you as the adult who will finally certify an identity and end the uncertainty. Feel that pull to name it, then refuse the role: most people first recognize a same-sex orientation in adolescence, and your job is to stay curious rather than become the labeler.

2009-297.sentence: Mesial temporal sclerosis—hippocampal atrophy plus T2 hyperintensity—is doing explanatory work the failed drugs cannot: it locates the seizures in a scarred memory circuit instead of in “nonadherence.” Once the MRI names the lesion, the team can stop treating the patient as morally stubborn and start talking about epilepsy surgery.

2009-298.sentence: The proud announcement is a wish for recognition colliding with an old prohibition against needing anything from you. Offer congratulations first: that gratifies the wish in reality so you do not enact the critic by going silent, interpreting the need, or auditing the grades.

2010-1.sentence: Telling the worker up front that this exam isn't confidential is what keeps the relationship honest — he needs to know you're working for the employer here, not for him, so he doesn't mistake this for a treatment alliance you never actually offered.

2010-2.sentence: Getting the phone number and address first stops the enactment: you refuse to become the helpless listener while command hallucinations keep running the scene. Location is how you leave the two-person panic and put a real body on a map instead of trading threats about police or quizzes about drugs.

2010-3.sentence: Digit span is the mind still here: six numbers held and handed back before they fall through. Immediate recall is not yesterday’s dinner or school history; it tests whether attention stayed in the chair or left without standing up.

2010-6.sentence: Rett disorder can look like something went wrong on a parent's watch — a child who was developing normally starts losing hand skills and words — but the regression is genetic (MECP2), not something anyone did. Naming it that way to the family is as much the job as naming the diagnosis itself.

2010-7.sentence: The 1974 DSM-II revision that dropped homosexuality is a frame decision: the profession, not the patient, decides what counts as illness and what stays off the chart. Read that change as an ethics of the limit—who holds the diagnostic boundary—rather than as proof that an identity was ever a disease or that a later edition made it vanish.

2010-11.sentence: Needle exchange is a two-person deal: you stay in the relationship while the patient is still injecting, instead of making abstinence the price of contact. Harm reduction here is interpersonal work—you and the patient build a pattern that reduces HIV and hepatitis risk together, rather than you holding a one-person demand they cannot yet meet.

2010-14.sentence: In autism the social cue is often not registered, so there is nothing to turn away from. Dissociation is a later, more expensive move: the child leaves the scene while still in the chair. PTSD, depression, and social phobia still track faces; they just cannot stay with what they see.

2010-16.sentence: Insurers pay most often for patient self-harm, not for sex, fraud, or a missed side effect. Denial is the defense that makes this statistic: if the wish to die is treated as noise rather than the central risk, the chart looks calm while the danger stays live. Thorough suicide documentation is suppression done right—you keep the threat in view instead of wishing it gone.

2010-17.sentence: Kraepelin’s gift was course: some psychoses remit between mood episodes, others grind into deficit. Self-esteem in a young psychiatrist often hangs on an idealized ancestor who can tell those stories apart. You borrow his longitudinal eye so you do not confuse a recoverable illness with one that will need a longer, humbler frame.

2010-18.sentence: Most homicide is ordinary rage, jealousy, and intoxication, not paranoid psychosis. The countertransference trap is to become the expert who locates the danger only in Axis I, because that role feels safer than facing a non-ill person who can still kill. Stay with threats, weapons, and the story of the slight; do not recruit yourself as the one who “explains it away” as illness.

2010-21.sentence: When a caregiver sometimes yields after saying no, that occasional yes is intermittent reinforcement. The child keeps seeking the person as a regulator because the slot machine still pays, which is why the behavior resists extinction.

2010-23.sentence: A securely attached 4-year-old who bargains for one more story is using language to delay a ordinary conflict, not leaving the room in a split. That is development doing its job: words instead of collapse or triangulation.

2010-24.sentence: Narcissistic exploitativeness treats the other person as a selfobject, a function to be used, not a mind with a claim. The coworkers who finish his work are proof of entitlement, not partners in a relationship.

2010-27.sentence: You hold the frame first: a private room, names, each step named before it happens, no one entering unasked. Legal talk, referrals, and guilt work wait until safety is actually restored; rushing them is another loss of control.

2010-28.sentence: The daughter brings the infidelity talk as something to evacuate—get rid of it with risperidone 0.5 while donepezil stays. Containing it means you sit with the raw dread of a fading spouse, keep regular visits, and let the fluctuating Alzheimer accusation become thinkable instead of a pill.

2010-29.sentence: Your capacity exam for this refusal can be finished today; competency cannot. Only a judicial hearing ends or limits that legal status, and no petition, neuropsych battery, or attorney letter can rush that ending.

2010-31.sentence: The family already cast this adolescent as clumsy; after the grand mal they recruit you as either the next adult who shrugs off the morning jerks or the one who names juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. Notice if you feel pulled to over-reassure so they stop looking frightened, or to over-investigate so you never have to sit with their shame about dropped objects.

2010-33.sentence: The wish is to be the one therapist who holds the adolescent and the family at once; the prohibition is the dual-relationship rule that those two jobs cannot occupy the same person. The symptom of saying yes is a compromise: you gratify the rescue wish and then leak confidentiality across rooms you were never meant to sit in together.

2010-34.sentence: Indiscriminate warmth after early foster-care disruption is not extra love; it is a child who cannot wait for a selective attachment to ripen. Reactive attachment disorder here is a limit problem: closeness with strangers comes cheap because the capacity for one enduring other cannot be rushed on the school’s timetable.

2010-35.sentence: Transient global amnesia dumps a raw “why am I in the hospital” that will not become a story; the patient evacuates it by asking again instead of thinking it. Your job is containment: you hold the repeating question and the intact recognition of family so the blank last two hours stay thinkable and do not turn into nameless dread.

2010-36.sentence: Group therapy is the frame that refuses the schizoid bargain of perfect fantasy friends and no real ones. The other members, the clock, and the room are the ethical limit: relatedness has to happen with actual people, not only inside the elaborate inner cast.

2010-38.sentence: Calling this “somatoform pain” when the tongue is large and percussion myoedema is sitting there is denial: you refuse the medical fact because a tidy psych label is less frightening. Name the hypothyroidism first; then you can talk about mood and aching without using a diagnosis as a cover.

2010-39.sentence: Each visit and each negative scan functions as a demand and a proof of need: the body must be gravely ill or the care would not be deserved. Insight is poor here, so do not argue the hypochondriasis away; offer a regular appointment as a reliable feed rather than another hunt for the hidden lesion.

2010-41.sentence: Secondary gain is the distinguishing motive in malingering; factitious disorder is after the sick role itself. Contain that raw mix—money, disability talk, fear of being seen as a fake—until a thinkable wish can be named, instead of evacuating the consult as “just malingering.”

2010-43.sentence: The staff’s “drug-seeking” story is a trial comment you can test with them: can they see their own part—fear of being used—without dumping it onto the patient? Methadone maintenance covers withdrawal, not cancer pain, so the useful interpretation is of the team, not of the request: give more opioid because tolerance is real.

2010-44.sentence: The frame is the set of limits that keep the work a treatment: time, fee, place, confidentiality. Homemade cookies near termination are a modest, one-time crossing of that frame; stretching the hour, café sessions with a borderline patient, investment tips as payment, and “anger means you’re fired” are violations that serve the therapist’s need, not the work.

2010-45.sentence: The Rorschach is the least structured test: an inkblot with almost no instruction becomes whatever the patient needs it to be—feed, poison, demand, or proof they are seen. MMPI, WAIS-III, TAT, and sentence completion still hand the patient a story, item, or stem; the blot hands them a blank and asks who they are with you.

2010-47.sentence: If the team keeps asking only for first-grade, grandma’s summer, the first sled ride, or a TV gag, they are enacting “prove you remember us”—a two-person repetition of reunion, not a memory exam. Semantic memory is the shared calendar fact: the town parade is every July 4th; that is knowledge, not a scene with you.

2010-48.sentence: Factitious disorder is organized around assuming the sick role, not around money, a hidden “real” diagnosis, or beating the doctor. The cultural third is the hospital’s hierarchy of worthy patients: illness as identity when other identities feel unlivable.

2010-51.sentence: One rejection letter and the student recruits you as the next admissions office: you will either bless or crush the whole future. Name the distortion—overgeneralization and all-or-none thinking—so you stay a therapist who thinks with the student, not another verdict.

2010-54.sentence: The record has to show why you rejected alternative ways of responding—hospitalize, restrain, send home—because every choice is also an ending of the other paths. You cannot rush that limit: write the reasons you did not take the unused roads, so the note holds the stop as well as the plan.

2010-56.sentence: Those rapidly shifting, shallow emotions are a bid for mirroring: the self feels real only when the room lights up. Idealizing the audience props self-esteem that does not hold from the inside, which is why histrionic affect looks theatrical and does not last.

2010-58.sentence: Rapport is what keeps the patient from splitting you into 'useless' or 'out to get me' — the ease, the compassion, the genuine curiosity about their view, and the quiet competence are what make you safe enough to actually work with, not just talk to.

2010-59.sentence: Develop discrepancy means holding up the gap between the life the patient wants and what the addiction is costing them, without you being the one who calls it wrong — confrontation invites defense, but hearing their own ambivalence out loud is what invites change.

2010-61.sentence: A random-assault survivor often still has a self that can use you as a mirror: someone who sees their courage as they approach the memory, rather than as a collapsed ideal. That leftover self-esteem is why graded exposure can land as competence work instead of another shattering.

2010-62.sentence: When you hold three words across a few minutes, you are not only scoring short-term memory; you are briefly the person who might forget them too. Notice if you rush the delay or over-coach—countertransference often wants to rescue the exam so neither of you feels dumb.

2010-63.sentence: Interferon-induced depression is not a footnote on a side-effect list — it can carry real suicidal risk, so when a patient on interferon reports despair, take it exactly as seriously as despair that arrived without a drug behind it.

2010-64.sentence: A six-year-old exploring genitals in the tub is ordinary phallic-stage curiosity, not a dissociative reenactment of abuse. Shame from the adult is what splits the child from the body; a calm privacy rule keeps the experience thinkable and owned.

2010-66.sentence: Ambivalence after a near-lethal overdose, a thin “I am sorry,” and no regret for surviving is raw dread that cannot yet be thought—Bion’s nameless stuff looking for a container. Inpatient hospitalization is that container: you hold the impulse in a locked frame until it can become a feeling instead of another evacuation.

2010-68.sentence: Informed consent for something this irreversible isn't about listing every risk you can imagine — it's the reasonable-patient standard: give the information a typical person facing this decision would need to actually decide for themselves.

2010-69.sentence: Kohut’s self psychology is not drive conflict or Erikson’s epigenetic stages; it is the need for empathic interaction with self-objects, people who lend cohesion when the self wobbles. When the resident misses a real accomplishment, the hurt is often a selfobject failure: the patient needed to be seen, not analyzed as vanity.

2010-73.sentence: Klein’s depressive position is the capacity to see a loved person as both good and harmed, then feel guilt and want to repair. A trial comment that names the patient’s own fury and the wish to make it right tests whether they can use that insight instead of only punishing themselves.

2010-74.sentence: A delusion isn't a distorted memory or a misread object — it's a fixed belief no evidence can touch, and for this patient it's also lived terror. You don't argue him out of it or play along; you stay with the fear underneath the belief, since that's what he can actually let you help with.

2010-76.sentence: Parent management training works because the child’s oppositional battles are often a bid for a coherent response when praise and limits have gone missing. Mirroring here is not flattery; it is the parent noticing competence and setting a firm frame so self-esteem is earned, not extracted by winning the fight.

2010-80.sentence: Voices arguing about the patient in the third person recruit you into the same triangle: two others deciding who he is while he listens. Notice the pull to become the third voice—the one who judges, sides, or silences—before you start documenting Schneider.

2010-84.sentence: IPT's middle phase deliberately stays on current relationships, not the transference or the childhood roots of a pattern — the idea is that mood improves by changing how a real relationship is going right now, not by understanding where the pattern came from.

2010-87.sentence: The conference podium turns the audience into a live conscience: tremor and tachycardia become proof that the trainee is about to be found wanting. Atenolol, taken shortly before exposure, lowers that bodily exhibit so the superego cannot use the heart as a gavel.

2010-88.sentence: Admission is not the hour to excavate death anxiety; the mind that just lost home needs information, not uncovering. Naming the living will as optional paper—not a demand to refuse treatment—keeps the work supportive and inside what an eighty-year-old in transition can use.

2010-89.sentence: At nine, Kohlberg's stage means right and wrong still lives outside the child, in whether an adult is watching to punish — not yet an internalized conscience the child carries alone. That's obedience to avoid consequence, not yet guilt.

2010-91.sentence: Learned helplessness is operant: after the environment stops pairing effort with any change in outcome, the person stops emitting the response that used to look like trying. The “symptom” is not laziness; it is a learned shutdown of agency that once protected them from more failed attempts.

2010-92.sentence: The break itself becomes part of the therapy — spend the leftover time on what it felt like to be asked to wait, not on catching up the agenda, because repairing that small rupture in trust is the real work the interruption just handed you.

2010-93.sentence: AACAP still wants a distinct period of abnormal mood with episodic symptoms, not a temperament that is always loud, frustrated, or culturally “too much.” If you collapse chronic irritability into bipolar I, you pathologize a child’s identity and environment instead of naming a true mood episode.

2010-94.sentence: Beneficence justifies paternalism only for as long as the patient genuinely can't act in their own interest — once capacity returns, staying protective stops being ethical and starts being control dressed up as care.

2010-95.sentence: This adoption study is the evidence for the disease model: biological risk for alcoholism travels through genes, not just through the household. That doesn't make it destiny — 'disease, not moral failing' is a reason to treat it seriously, not a reason to treat it as fixed.

2010-97.sentence: The depressive position is two-person work: you and the patient stop taking turns as the all-good or all-bad partner and practice staying in the room after a disappointment. Comfort with “the good with the bad” is not a solo insight; it is what happens when neither of you has to split the relationship to keep it from feeling ruined.

2010-98.sentence: Vertical-gaze slowing plus axial rigidity and falls is progressive supranuclear palsy, not garden-variety Parkinson disease, and the stay-at-home anxiety is often proximity-seeking after the body stopped being a secure base. Treat the fear of leaving as attachment protest to a failing motor system, not as a free-floating phobia you can talk away.

2010-100.sentence: Acculturation is keeping family recipes while taking up American ballroom dancing—heritage and host culture both stay live, which is not assimilation’s wipe-and-replace. In the room, culture is a third person: ask which practices still feed identity instead of assuming the dancing means the old self is gone.

2010-101.sentence: Before you can treat the substance use, you have to engage the teen and the family without anyone getting cast as the villain — parents who feel entitled to be furious, and a kid who already expects to be treated like 'the bad addict,' both need to be able to stay in the room as people, not roles.

2010-104.sentence: Caffeine intoxication here isn't just a stimulant tally — it's a physician trying to cover for a chronically understaffed shift with his own body, because no one has been willing to say out loud that the schedule itself is unsustainable.

2010-108.sentence: A negative therapeutic reaction is getting worse after an accurate, well-timed interpretation, not after a clumsy one. The self that needed to stay small cannot yet take in being understood; the insight lands as a blow to the old way of earning love.

2010-109.sentence: Control is this man's wish after the infarct: if he can interrogate every test and pill, he is not a passive body on the floor. The team answers the questions and pulls him into the plan so the wish can work in reality instead of colliding with a staff prohibition that would turn him into a defiant, refusing patient.

2010-110.sentence: Bilateral parotid enlargement is not just a gland finding; it is the body advertising a secret purge the patient cannot say. The swelling does work for the person: it lets vomiting stay unnamed while still marking the anorexia as a binge-purge pattern you must treat, not simple restriction.

2010-111.sentence: Winnicott's holding environment is the developmental capacity that arrives when parenting is consistent and reliable enough that the infant does not have to organize the world alone. If that safe context never quite arrives, later transitions feel like falling, and treatment starts by restoring predictability rather than interpreting content.

2010-113.sentence: Serial sevens recruit you as the examiner who will either stay with the patient's effort or grow impatient and fill in the numbers. Watch that countertransference: irritation at the slow 100-minus-7s is data about concentration, not a cue to abandon the task or treat it as a memory test.

2010-114.sentence: Khat wasn't 'a drug' in this man's life back home — it was concentration, sociability, and stamina for long workdays. If you only hear 'stimulant misuse,' he'll hear judgment of something that organized his life, not curiosity about it, and you'll lose the alliance you need to actually assess dependence.

2010-117.sentence: It's tempting to read a year without sex as a relationship problem, but vestibulodynia is a physical pain condition first — treat the pain before you treat the marriage, because meaningful couples work can't happen around touch that still genuinely hurts.

2010-119.sentence: A useful trial comment is: the fear is choking, not calories or shape—so this is specific phobia after one panic-while-eating episode, not an eating disorder or panic disorder. If they can see that the avoided pasta is a feared sensation in the throat, they have enough mind to work the phobia instead of shrinking the plate forever.

2010-120.sentence: The harsh superego—your inner rule-maker—wants to bar the spouse at the door in the name of purity and confidentiality. The grown-up frame is yes if the patient wishes, plus a later private hour: conscience that can make a sanctioned exception without handing the whole interview to the couple.

2010-122.sentence: A loss that never gets put into words doesn't just disappear — in a vulnerable brain it can resurface instead as a depressive episode, so when you take the history, ask what happened before you only ask about the mood.

2010-125.sentence: Numbing and then a surge of arousal is the old fight between a wish to vanish and a drive to stay ready after the knifepoint robbery. Call it acute stress disorder while it is still inside a month; the clock, not the flavor of dissociation, is what keeps it from being PTSD.

2010-128.sentence: The limit you hold is time, not another consult: functional blindness after a witnessed murder is expected to lift in days or weeks if you do not install a chronic-patient frame. Colluding with endless lesion-hunting or a sick role keeps the eyes in the job of not seeing; naming a short course lets the symptom finish and leave.

2010-129.sentence: A trial comment to the parents—that the new sibling took the old place and the accidents came back to reclaim it—lets them see the child's part without calling it delay or acting out. That is psychological mindedness in a three-year-old's language: normal regression after a successful toilet training, not a new diagnosis.

2010-130.sentence: The split is doing work: pills live in one office and meaning in the other, so anger never has to sit in one relationship. The psychiatrist's job is to evaluate need, prescribe, and keep regular contact with the therapist so the patient cannot park the conflict in the gap.

2010-133.sentence: This patient already expects to be written off as 'just here to get high' — take the back pain seriously anyway, because spinal epidural abscess is exactly the kind of catastrophic diagnosis that gets missed when stigma answers before the exam does.

2010-136.sentence: Tics live in a two-person field: shame, watching, and family alarm can amp the motor and vocal bursts as much as the basal ganglia do. When antipsychotics and alpha-2 agonists have already failed that shared pattern, tetrabenazine is the next move you make with a tic specialist, not another round of “try harder” at home.

2010-138.sentence: Conjoint marital therapy asks for ego strengths the violent partner does not have in the room: impulse control, affect tolerance, and a shared reality that the other person is not property. Put them together and you get an enactment of coercion, not treatment; start with private individual work and safety.

2010-141.sentence: Combativeness in Alzheimer disease often means the daughter's adult capacity to hold a parent has been exceeded, not that the 80-year-old can still learn from time-outs or a changing schedule. Assessing caregiver burnout names the developmental mismatch: the child-as-parent is exhausted, and that exhaustion is the intervention target if home care is to continue.

2010-143.sentence: Attribution is the story you tell yourself about why something happened — internal, global, and stable versus specific and one-off — and that story does real work: explaining a mistake as 'I am incompetent' forever, versus 'I missed this one thing,' shapes whether the next mistake feels survivable.

2010-144.sentence: Amphetamine had been a cheap selfobject: it mirrored energy and competence until the crash. Dysphoria and anhedonia after the high usually need 2 to 4 months to ease, so the empty, unmirrored self is not a one- or two-week dip you can pep-talk away.

2010-145.sentence: Mature object relations means this mourner can hold love and anger toward the same lost person without collapsing, so STPP can work the real collision: the wish to stay fused with the dead versus the prohibition on rage, guilt, and letting go. Supportive therapy soothes that conflict; STPP interprets it, which is why those patients outperform supportive care in complicated grief—and why male gender, age, and meds do not pick the winner.

2010-146.sentence: The opening line recruits you as the spouse’s enforcer—the person who will complete an evaluation someone else already decided. Asking “How do you feel about that?” refuses that transference role and puts the patient’s own affect, not the spouse’s mandate, in the chair; dates, the spouse’s treatment history, and joking that your spouse advises you too all keep you as the spouse’s stand-in.

2010-154.sentence: Ethnicity, unlike race or SES, is the shared history the work cannot rush past if you want a real ending with this person. Asking about ancestry, beliefs, and the language at home honors a limit: identity is not a demographic you assign and then terminate the conversation.

2010-156.sentence: The frame for a five-year-old after a move is time and a holding limit, not a report that development was lost. Transient thumb-sucking and accidents are regression inside a still-maturing child; you hold the hour and the story rather than treating earlier behaviors as a broken milestone.

2010-157.sentence: The CRAFFT car question is not small talk; it asks whether the teen will let a substance sit in the driver's seat of a real body. Naming that risk out loud can feel like a demand or a feed: you are offering protection, and they may hear you taking away the high or calling them needy.

2010-160.sentence: Frotteurism is the urge to rub against a nonconsenting stranger, often on a crowded train, and the distress does not make the act a medicine. Treat any later SSRI or antiandrogen as a limit you two negotiate, not a chemical fig leaf that proves the patient is either poisoned or finally “fixed.”

2010-161.sentence: Supervision belongs in the opening frame, same as fee and time: the patient deserves to know a third person already sits in the room. Hiding the attending until they ask is not kindness; it is you holding the confidentiality limit for your comfort instead of theirs.

2010-162.sentence: Naming deficits after cueing point to cortical language loss, not the give-up-and-slow-down of depression. If you keep treating only the lifelong mood and skip that anomia, you and the family are already in an enactment: repeating “it’s just the depression” instead of facing a new brain.

2010-163.sentence: Calling this 'just a bad migraine' is denial doing its job — it buys you a calmer minute, but a young adult with sudden drowsiness and bilateral Babinski signs needs a scan, not reassurance, and denial is expensive when it delays that.

2010-165.sentence: Praise and an upcoming vacation work as a mirror: someone else briefly holds this person’s worth, so mood lifts and the sweet binge can pause. Fear of rejection is the same self-esteem system with the mirror gone—intimacy feels like a drop, not a relationship.

2010-166.sentence: Flumazenil can reverse alprazolam at the GABA-A receptor; it cannot make the patient see their part in emptying the bottle. After the airway is safe, one trial comment—“what was happening that you needed this much?”—tests whether they can use insight or only the antidote.

2010-167.sentence: Oppositional defiant disorder lives at the limit: “no,” bedtime, and adult time are endings the child cannot yet metabolize, so anger and blame arrive instead of a stop. You do not rush that capacity with a lecture; you hold a firm, boring frame until “stop” is thinkable.

2010-168.sentence: On a blot or TAT card the patient can park a bad object—persecutor, fragment, bizarre link—without having to keep good and bad in one relationship the way interview requires. That is why projective testing can catch a subtle psychotic process the mental status still packages as “a bit guarded.”

2010-172.sentence: Privilege belongs to the patient, not to the judge, the psychiatrist, or the DA who wants the chart. That is the frame: the resident does not mail records on a subpoena alone, because handing over the file as if it were yours is a boundary break dressed as cooperation.

2010-173.sentence: Past violent behavior predicts future violence better than anger, weapons, or which defense you name on the board.
